text:
Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns, who wandered far and wide after he had sacked the holy citadel of Troy. Many were the cities of men he saw and knew their minds, and many were the pains he suffered in his heart upon the open sea, striving to win his own life and the return of his companions. Yet not even so did he save his comrades, for all his longing: through their own reckless folly they perished — fools, who devoured the cattle of Helios Hyperion; and he took from them the day of their return. From some point of this, goddess, daughter of Zeus, speak to us too.

Then all the rest, as many as had fled sheer destruction, were now at home, having escaped war and the sea. But that one man alone, who longed for his return and for his wife, the queenly nymph Calypso, shining among goddesses, held back in her hollow caves, yearning for him to be her husband. But when the year arrived in the circling of the seasons in which the gods had spun for him to return home to Ithaca, not even there was he free of trials, even among his own people. And all the gods pitied him, except Poseidon; he raged unceasingly against godlike Odysseus until he reached his own land.

But Poseidon had gone among the Ethiopians, who dwell far off — the Ethiopians, divided in two, the farthest of men, some where Hyperion sets and some where he rises — to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams. There he sat at the feast and took his pleasure. But the others were gathered together in the halls of Olympian Zeus. And among them the father of men and gods began speaking; for he called to mind in his heart blameless Aegisthus, whom far-famed Orestes, son of Agamemnon, had slain. Thinking of him, he spoke these words among the immortals:
review_notes: English translation of Homer, Odyssey, Book 1, lines 1–32, translated directly from the Ancient Greek source (Oxford Classical Text, Allen, 1917). The translation prioritizes semantic fidelity over poetic meter: the dactylic hexameter is rendered as rhythmical prose that preserves the narrative sequence, epithets, and divine-mortal dynamics. Key choices: 'man of many turns' for πολύτροπον (capturing both 'much-wandering' and 'many-deviced' meanings), 'reckless folly' for ἀτασθαλίῃσιν (the Homeric term for morally culpable foolishness), 'shining among goddesses' for δῖα θεάων (preserving the visual-numinous quality of the epithet), 'raging unceasingly' for ἀσπερχὲς μενέαινεν. The epithets of Odysseus ('godlike'), Calypso ('queenly nymph'), and Aegisthus ('blameless') are rendered consistently. The transition from the Muse invocation to the narrative exposition and then to Zeus's speech is preserved as a single continuous passage. The hecatomb scene retains the ethnographic-geographic specificity of the original.
